results.name: same_decade_near_contrast
results.description: For non-example targets 1-5 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens decade (floor((n-1)/10)) minus when it crosses a decade boundary; observed above the null means people treat decades as category boundaries that the model's boundary-free intervals ignore (below = no such boundary effect, less than model).
results.code:
# name: same_decade_near_contrast
# description: For non-example targets 1-5 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens decade (floor((n-1)/10)) minus when it crosses a decade boundary; observed above the null means people treat decades as category boundaries that the model's boundary-free intervals ignore (below = no such boundary effect, less than model).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in sets.unique()}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    near = np.array([ex[s][np.argmin(np.abs(ex[s] - tt))] for s, tt in zip(sets, t)])
    d = np.abs(near - t)
    ok = (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)
    same = ok & ((near - 1) // 10 == (t - 1) // 10)
    cross = ok & ~same
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if same.sum() == 0 or cross.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[same].mean() - y[cross].mean())

results.name: multi_example_cluster_support
results.description: Among 3-4-example sets and non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 8 of two or more examples minus targets within 8 of exactly one example; observed above the null means similarity support sums across nearby examples more than the model's interval/rule posterior implies (below = less density sensitivity than the model).
results.code:
# name: multi_example_cluster_support
# description: Among 3-4-example sets and non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 8 of two or more examples minus targets within 8 of exactly one example; observed above the null means similarity support sums across nearby examples more than the model's interval/rule posterior implies (below = less density sensitivity than the model).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in sets.unique()}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = np.array([len(ex[s]) for s in sets])
    dmin = np.array([np.abs(ex[s] - tt).min() for s, tt in zip(sets, t)])
    cnt = np.array([int((np.abs(ex[s] - tt) <= 8).sum()) for s, tt in zip(sets, t)])
    ok = (n >= 3) & (dmin > 0)
    a, b = ok & (cnt >= 2), ok & (cnt == 1)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_tolerant_rule_yes
results.description: Among 3-4-example sets where no rule of size <=25 (multiples of 3-50, ends-in-digit, squares, powers of 2/3) fits all examples but one fits all but one, yes rate for non-example targets in that smallest leave-one-out rule; observed above the null means people discount a single outlier example and still follow the rule more than the model's random-example noise allows (below = they abandon the rule more readily).

results.name: small_vs_large_absolute_far_target
results.description: For targets more than 15 away from every example, yes rate for targets 1-20 minus targets 81-100 (absolute magnitude, not relative to examples); observed above the null means people favour small numbers as generic program outputs beyond what the model's concepts and uniform noise produce (below = favour large numbers).

results.name: divisibility_relation_far_contrast
results.description: For non-example targets >=2 that are more than 10 away from every example, yes rate when the target divides or is a multiple of at least one example (pairwise divisibility) minus when it has no such relation; observed above the null means people generalize via pairwise arithmetic relations to single examples beyond the model's whole-set rules (below = less).
results.code:
# name: divisibility_relation_far_contrast
# description: For non-example targets >=2 that are more than 10 away from every example, yes rate when the target divides or is a multiple of at least one example (pairwise divisibility) minus when it has no such relation; observed above the null means people generalize via pairwise arithmetic relations to single examples beyond the model's whole-set rules (below = less).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in sets.unique()}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    dist = np.array([np.abs(ex[s] - tt).min() for s, tt in zip(sets, t)])
    rel = np.array([bool(np.any((ex[s] % tt == 0) | (tt % ex[s] == 0))) for s, tt in zip(sets, t)])
    ok = (dist > 10) & (t >= 2)
    a, b = ok & rel, ok & ~rel
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: first_vs_repeat_set_exposure
results.description: Yes rate on a participant's first trial with a given set (participant = run starting at trial_index 0) minus yes rate on later trials with that same set, non-example targets only; the model treats every trial independently, so observed above the null means generalization narrows with repeated exposure to a set (below = it broadens).
results.code:
# name: first_vs_repeat_set_exposure
# description: Yes rate on a participant's first trial with a given set (participant = run starting at trial_index 0) minus yes rate on later trials with that same set, non-example targets only; the model treats every trial independently, so observed above the null means generalization narrows with repeated exposure to a set (below = it broadens).
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].to_numpy() == 0).cumsum()
    key = pd.Series(pid).astype(str) + "|" + df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    k = pd.Series(key.to_numpy()).groupby(key.to_numpy()).cumcount().to_numpy()
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str).to_numpy()
    inset = np.array([tt in s.split(",") for tt, s in zip(t, sets)])
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = (k == 0) & ~inset, (k > 0) & ~inset
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: mixed_parity_even_target_bias
results.description: Among sets containing both odd and even examples, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; the model has no parity preference once examples mix parity, so observed away from the null means people carry a residual parity bias (above = even favoured, below = odd favoured) the model misses.
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_even_target_bias
# description: Among sets containing both odd and even examples, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; the model has no parity preference once examples mix parity, so observed away from the null means people carry a residual parity bias (above = even favoured, below = odd favoured) the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    mixed = {s: len({int(x) % 2 for x in s.split(",")}) == 2 for s in sets.unique()}
    mx = sets.map(mixed).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    inset = np.array([str(tt) in s.split(",") for tt, s in zip(t, sets)])
    ok = mx & ~inset
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = ok & (t % 2 == 0), ok & (t % 2 == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: nonzero_residue_class_contrast
results.description: Among 2+-example sets whose examples all share a nonzero residue r mod k for some k in {3,4,6,7,8,9,11,12} (largest such k; e.g. odd multiples of 3 = 3 mod 6), yes rate for non-example targets with the same residue minus targets with a different residue; observed above the null means people infer offset/intersection concepts ("odd multiples of 3") the model's zero-residue multiples rules lack (below = less than the model).
